summary: The recommended architecture is a batch EL pipeline with object storage landing and a warehouse load job, because a daily run with a 2-hour SLA does not require streaming complexity.
decision: Use a daily architecture: Salesforce API → scheduled extractor (Airbyte/Fivetran or custom) → object storage (Parquet) → warehouse load job → staging → mart. Enforce idempotent partition loads and produce both a data contract and runbook deliverable.
rationale: This architecture aligns with the SLA while minimizing operational overhead. It supports fail-loud behavior through explicit validation checks and predictable retries. The data contract defines schema and ownership boundaries; the runbook defines alerting, backfill, and incident response.

tradeOffs.pros: Simpler operations, lower cost, easier backfill

costEstimate: Daily extract of typical Salesforce object volumes (≤1M rows/day) lands well under one warehouse credit-hour per run; storage in object landing ≈ 5–10 GB per object per month at standard Parquet compression. Validate against your specific volume and retention policy before sign-off.

risks.description: Salesforce API rate limits can cause partial daily extracts during peak load.
risks.mitigation: Set retries=3 with exponential backoff (W006); fall back to bulk API for >100K-row pulls; alert on partial completion via row-count parity check.

risks.description: Schema drift in Salesforce custom fields can break the contract silently.
risks.mitigation: Pin the contract to fields the consumer actually uses; treat new custom fields as additive (W004) and drop them at the staging boundary unless explicitly added to the contract.

nextSteps: Finalize source objects, destination tables, and daily load window.
Draft and approve the data contract with schema, SLAs, and ownership.
Implement the runbook with escalation, retries, and backfill procedure.
Add idempotent partition overwrite and row-count reconciliation checks.
